thread.title: 5 sleeper stocks that will win from this year’s hot tech trends

author: Daniel Newman
title: 5 sleeper stocks that will win from this year’s hot tech trends
text:
The search for value is constant, but sometimes the value in innovation outside of a handful of technology stocks gets little attention.
But with artificial intelligence, Internet of Things, 5G and Edge Computing all driving massive investment, some less-hyped tech companies should do well this year. I’m bullish on the technology that plays into these hot trends and the sales and earnings they will generate for these five sleeper stocks.
Dell Technologies: This company DELL, -3.76% which returned to the stock market in December, has spent the past five years building arguably the most complete set of enterprise technology solutions. Following the acquisition of EMC and VMware, Dell made a number of other strategic acquisitions in security and data, including RSA, Pivotal and Boomi. With even closer integration between the business units, Dell Tech stands to see meaningful growth as customers invest in infrastructure to support their enterprise needs. Investors who didn’t track Dell during the past five years may still see it as a big consumer PC company and not realize how different it is today,
Qualcomm: This is the year that 5G goes from hype to reality, and Qualcomm QCOM, -0.35% is very much at the center of this new cellphone technology. With significant contributions to the 5G NR (New Radio) standard , Qualcomm is certain to see an uptick in business as carriers, infrastructure providers and consumers all race to be part of the 5G buzz. More than 30 commitments to use its new Snapdragon 855 5G mobile platform were announced at CES 2019 this month. But investors recently have been down on Qualcomm, in part because of disappointing earnings and its continuing legal fight with Apple AAPL, -1.50% and may not fully appreciate how much 5G will boost sales this year.
Texas Instruments: Texas Instruments TXN, -2.29% has nearly 70% of the analog chip market. In a digital world, that may not seem like too exciting. However, analog chips are critical to the rapidly growing Internet of Things. What many investors don’t realize is that analog sensors that collect temperature, speed, sound and current are necessary to feed the digital chips that will process and convert this data into information on the network. Basically, sales of TI’s analog sensors should increase alongside the expected growth in IoT and digital semiconductors.
Applied Materials: While some analysts have been somewhat hard on the semiconductor industry , I don’t see chip sales slowing anytime soon. Applied Materials doesn’t make chips, but rather provides materials to chip makers. If you agree with me that chip sales are set to rise, then those providing materials are likely beneficiaries. As a bonus for those willing to take a risk on Applied Materials, the stock slumped 40% last year, ending the year at $32.74 and has recovered only modestly so far this year.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise: Unlike Dell Tech and its massive portfolio, HPE HPE, -0.56% narrowed its focus following its split from Hewlett-Packard Co. HPQ, -1.79% and the PC business. For me, HPE is out-innovating the competition in two areas. Its Greenlake IT service offerings integrate smart metering so enterprises can pay for only the amount of IT services consumed. Second, its Edgeline line of specially designed servers for industrial applications and Aruba wireless networking solutions means it has the most complete offering and what I believe to be the most innovative hardware to support investments in Edge computing, one of the hottest tech trends of 2019. Edge computing is all about processing data closer to where it is being created to improve the speed that data is turned into insights. Autonomous vehicles, smart cities, digital factories and mobile telecommunications are just a few of the areas using it.
Daniel Newman is the principal analyst at Futurum Research . Follow him on Twitter @danielnewmanUV .
